title: Architecture Evolution
subtitle: Change service boundaries from measured ownership and scaling constraints
objectives: Prefer explicit modules before distributed services
Use the strangler pattern for incremental replacement
Define service ownership around data and invariants
Recognize distributed costs introduced by a split

exercises.title: A modular monolith can enforce ownership boundaries without network calls
exercises.body: Separate responsibilities through module APIs and data ownership before distributing them across processes. A process split adds independent deployment and scaling only when those benefits justify network failure, operational overhead, and cross-service consistency work.
exercises.note: Code organization and runtime topology are different decisions; one does not require the other.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: A modular monolith can enforce ownership boundaries without network calls
exercises.why: Separate responsibilities through module APIs and data ownership before distributing them across processes. A process split adds independent deployment and scaling only when those benefits justify network failure, operational overhead, and cross-service consistency work. Code organization and runtime topology are different decisions; one does not require the other.

exercises.prompt: A 6-person team has one application, shared tables, and unclear ownership. Deployments are fast and load is modest. Improve boundaries without adding network operations.
choices: Split into 20 services immediately
Define module APIs and table ownership inside the application
Let every feature update every table
choiceFeedback: Twenty services add coordination and operations without evidence that independent runtime scaling is needed.
Owned modules clarify responsibility while preserving simple local calls and transactions.
Shared mutation keeps coupling and makes invariants ownerless.
exercises.beforeStatus: CHANGE IMPACT · every feature can modify every table
exercises.afterStatus: CHANGE IMPACT · module APIs protect owned invariants
exercises.why: Module boundaries create explicit contracts and ownership without partial network failure or distributed transactions. Later evidence can justify extracting one module while preserving the established boundary.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A 6-person team has one application, shared tables, and unclear ownership. Deployments are fast and load is modest. Improve boundaries without adding network operations. Place Owned tables. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Orders module → Owned tables; Payments module → Owned tables. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Module boundaries create explicit contracts and ownership without partial network failure or distributed transactions. Later evidence can justify extracting one module while preserving the established boundary.

exercises.prompt: Which evidence can justify extracting a module into a service? Select all.
choices: It needs materially different scaling
A team needs independent deployment ownership
Its availability or security boundary differs
Microservices appear modern
exercises.why: Independent scaling, ownership, availability, or security can repay distribution cost. Fashion does not define a workload or organizational constraint.

exercises.title: The strangler pattern moves one route or capability at a time
exercises.body: Place a routing boundary in front of the old system, implement one capability in the new path, compare behavior, and move traffic gradually. The legacy path remains available for rollback until the migrated capability is verified.
exercises.note: Data ownership must move deliberately; routing traffic alone can leave two systems writing the same invariant.

exercises.prompt: A two-year rewrite plans one final cutover of the entire billing system. Reduce the failure scope and time before evidence.
choices: Wait for the complete rewrite
Route one bounded capability to the new service and compare outcomes
Write every request to both systems without an authority rule
choiceFeedback: A final cutover concentrates integration, data, and rollback risk into one event.
A bounded capability creates production evidence and a reversible traffic boundary.
Uncontrolled dual authority creates conflicting state.
exercises.beforeStatus: CUTOVER · all capabilities change in one irreversible event
exercises.afterStatus: CUTOVER · one route moves · measured rollback remains
exercises.result: Migration risk is bounded by one capability
exercises.why: Incremental routing limits blast radius and makes rollback a traffic decision. The migrated service needs one authoritative data-write path and reconciliation for any shadow comparison.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: A two-year rewrite plans one final cutover of the entire billing system. Reduce the failure scope and time before evidence. Place Capability router, Legacy, New invoicing. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Billing traffic → Capability router; Capability router → Legacy; Capability router → New invoicing. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Incremental routing limits blast radius and makes rollback a traffic decision. The migrated service needs one authoritative data-write path and reconciliation for any shadow comparison.

steps: Define the capability and its data owner
Implement and shadow the new path
Move a small traffic share and compare evidence
Expand traffic, remove the old path, then clean up
exercises.why: Ownership and a seam precede implementation; shadowing and staged traffic provide evidence; cleanup waits until the old path is no longer a rollback dependency.

exercises.title: A service split converts local assumptions into distributed protocols
exercises.body: A function call becomes a network request with deadlines and retries; one transaction becomes a workflow; a shared schema becomes versioned APIs and events; debugging requires cross-service context. Record these costs in the extraction decision.
exercises.note: Independent deployment is valuable only when contracts and data ownership let teams change independently in practice.

exercises.prompt: Match each local assumption to its distributed replacement.

pairs.right: Network call with timeout and retry policy

exercises.why: Distribution introduces partial failure, independent commits, and fragmented evidence. Each local mechanism needs an explicit distributed replacement rather than an unchanged interface name.

exercises.prompt: Orders and inventory change together in one small team's application, share one scaling profile, and require atomic reservation. Choose the boundary emphasis.
exercises.leftLabel: Keep owned modules in one deployable
exercises.why: Shared ownership, scaling, and atomic invariants favor a local module boundary. Extraction becomes stronger when independent scaling or ownership evidence outweighs workflow and network complexity.

exercises.title: A service boundary is incomplete until one owner controls each write
exercises.body: Moving code behind a network endpoint does not create an independent service while both the monolith and new service write the same tables. Extraction needs an authority transition: route new writes to one owner, migrate historical data, reconcile differences, then remove the old writer.
exercises.note: Shared reads may remain temporarily. Two uncoordinated writers create ambiguous invariants, rollback, and incident ownership.

exercises.prompt: The Orders service has its own deployment, but the monolith still updates the same order rows directly. What has actually been extracted?
choices: A fully independent service
A network API, but not exclusive data ownership
An event stream
A disaster-recovery system
exercises.why: Deployment separation does not establish authority. While two codebases can mutate the same records, either can violate the other's assumptions and neither owns the write invariant end to end.

exercises.prompt: Order a reversible strangler extraction for order writes.
steps: Define the new service contract and ownership invariant
Route a small cohort of writes through the new service
Compare outcomes and reconcile migrated state
Increase traffic while monitoring correctness and latency
Remove the monolith's direct write path after rollback closes
exercises.why: The sequence establishes the contract before moving authority, limits blast radius during observation, and removes the old writer only after evidence and rollback requirements permit it.

exercises.prompt: Which signals justify splitting a module into a separately deployed service? Select all.
choices: It needs independent scaling proven by measurements
A stable team can own its contract and data
Release coupling creates repeated operational pain
Microservices appear on an architecture diagram
exercises.why: A service boundary adds network, consistency, deployment, and observability costs. Independent scaling, ownership, or release constraints can repay that bill; fashion cannot.

exercises.prompt: Build the authority cutover. New writes go through one owner; an event updates the monolith's temporary read copy without giving it write authority.
exercises.why: The client sends mutations to the Orders service, which owns the authoritative database. Events may feed a temporary read copy, but the monolith cannot write back through that derived path.

exercises.prompt: A team moves invoice code into a separate process, but both the monolith and new service still mutate invoice tables. What remains unresolved?
choices: Whether invoices have IDs
Exclusive write ownership and invariant authority
Network connectivity
The programming language
exercises.why: A deployment boundary is not a data-ownership boundary. Two independent writers can violate each other's assumptions until one service owns authoritative mutations.
